explanation: A camel's humps are stores of fat it can live off when food is scarce. In a well-fed camel they stand firm and upright; in a starving one they shrink and flop over.

claims.text: A dromedary, or Arabian, camel has one hump.
A Bactrian camel has two humps.
Camel humps store fat that a camel can use when food is scarce.
The humps of a well-fed camel stand firm, while those of a starving camel shrink and flop over.

writerNotes: Self-check (guide 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true. The selfCheck field itself is left out because the CNT-1 item schema refuses it as an unknown key, so the codes are recorded here. lint: content:check reports no errors and no warnings for this item. claims: four listed; high: c1 (number, a comparison label) and c2 (number, a comparison label); standard: c3 and c4. datasets: no pinned dataset in content/datasets/manifest.json covers animal or plant biology (it holds countries, languages, currencies, cities, elements, Nobel Prizes, Olympic Games, World Cups, art collections and Natural Earth), so none applies, and the high-risk claims need web evidence from checker A; one search on dromedary and Bactrian humps should cover c1 and c2. rivalTest: Exact counts, so a difference of one is allowed by the separation guard. An easy item: the reasoning foothold is the old memory aid that a capital B lying on its side has two humps and a D has one. Hybrid camels were not considered because the labels name the two species. volatility: evergreen, a settled fact that cannot change; no time words, and nothing rests on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: dromedaries live from North Africa to India and Australia, Bactrians in Central Asia. style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens only, explanation of 33 words. myths: screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches. mystery and encore: nothing of either kind in a comparison item. doubts: none. The explanation says what humps store without mentioning water, so the claim never touches the camel-hump myth.
